Unobserved items are uncertain negatives: users may like products they have never encountered. UFNRec explicitly studies false negatives in sequential recommendation; GNNO uses training-sequence neighborhood overlap and an easy-to-hard curriculum, reporting improvements on three Amazon benchmarks. These support controlling negative difficulty, but do not establish that title similarity reliably identifies false negatives. ([UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116), [GNNO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10047))

Lexical similarity and model difficulty should be measured separately. Shared title words can flag possible duplicates, variants or substitutes; this is a heuristic, not evidence of user rejection or model confusion. Model difficulty depends on the current history-conditioned prediction score, positive–negative score gap or loss contribution. Google’s training guide defines hard negatives through high model scores. R2NS specifically motivates uniform-sampling warm-start followed by curriculum-controlled mining because introducing hard negatives too early can impair training. ([Google](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/recommendation/dnn/training), [R2NS](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf))

Practical ablation proposal: retain one HSTU per category; compare uniform sampling, text-selected negatives, model-scored moderate negatives, and uniform warm-start followed by a gradual hard-negative fraction. Exclude known training positives; optionally suppress near-duplicate candidates without changing benchmark candidates. Keep uniform coverage and avoid always selecting the highest-scoring unknown item. Log lexical overlap, score gaps, exclusion rates and training cost separately. Treat duplicate filtering and moderate-hardness thresholds as hypotheses requiring validation; select using the fixed macro validation HR@10, with no test-label access.
